extracted.intended_audience: startup founders, PR/marketing professionals, and communicators writing press releases aimed at journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting press releases and media pitches that are likely to be picked up by journalists, emphasizing journalist-focused framing, concise ledes, strong headlines, and correct distribution. Aimed at improving the odds a release will be opened and used by reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for the journalist (not the company)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most press releases are written for the company, not for the journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind reporters receive 200+ pitches per day, decide in ~4 seconds, and 92% of press releases get ignored. Prioritize the journalist's needs and a clear news angle rather than corporate messaging or vanity announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickup-Worthy Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing, ask three questions to judge whether the story is worth a release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions: 1) Would my mom find this interesting at dinner? 2) Does this affect more than just our customers? 3) If I were a reporter on deadline, would I bother my editor about this? If the answer is 'no' to all three — kill it. Don't write the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline rules that drive pickup
rubrics_metrics.description: How to craft a headline that gets opened and read by journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Front-load the news, not the brand name; include numbers when possible (e.g., 'Raises $20M', '3X faster'); avoid words like 'announces', 'unveils', 'is proud to' (these are red flags); keep headlines to 80 characters or less; pass the 'subject line test' — would you open this email?

rubrics_metrics.name: Lede paragraph formula
rubrics_metrics.description: A short, three-sentence lede that delivers the essential story quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentence 1: The single most newsworthy fact. Sentence 2: Why it matters to the reader (not your customers — the reader). Sentence 3: Concrete detail (number, date, person). Total: under 50 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: What journalists actually want
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements journalists need to run a story without heavy rewriting or chasing sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an angle they can run with (not boilerplate they must rewrite); include quotes that 'say something' — avoid platitudes like 'we are excited to'; make one spokesperson available NOW (not 'by appointment'); attach data, screenshots, photos; consider offering exclusivity (high value) or embargo (moderate value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flags that kill pickup
rubrics_metrics.description: Common phrases, formats, or omissions that cause journalists to ignore a release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid: 'Leading provider of...' in the boilerplate; hype words in headlines such as 'game-changing', 'revolutionary', 'disruptive'; releases longer than 600 words; CEO quotes that include the company name; no phone number; PDF-only attachments; and a dateline more than 24 hours old. Any of these can prevent pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred order and methods for distributing a press release to maximize pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order: 1) Direct, personalized email to 5–10 reporters who cover your beat; 2) Wire service (only if newsworthy enough to warrant it); 3) Newsroom on company site; 4) Social syndication; 5) Industry-specific aggregators. Personalization and targeted outreach are top priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit quality rubric (summary checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quick checklist of what makes a release high-quality and pickup-worthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real news, not a vanity announcement; headline tested against the 'subject line test'; lede under 50 words with concrete facts; quotes that humans actually said (meaningful and not generic); spokesperson genuinely available; multimedia attached rather than promised; personalized to the journalist's beat.
